item.title: Moose Movement in Relation to Roads
item.dc:creator: Galen Seilis
item.description:
A moose that walks onto a highway is a public-safety problem, a conservation problem, and a modelling problem all at once. Because a moose has a high centre of mass and long, brittle legs, a collision at highway speed sends the body through the windscreen rather than over the bonnet; in Maine, collisions with moose accounted for about 15% of reported animal collisions but roughly half of the human injuries and 14 of 17 fatalities over a five-year period (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2006). Reported counts exceed 800 collisions per year in Alaska alone (Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities 2018). The same animal is also, for most of the year, trying not to be near a road: roads carry traffic, hunters, and wolves, all of which raise mortality risk, yet roadsides offer salt, early green-up, and thin snow that lower foraging and travel costs. Moose movement in relation to roads is therefore not one phenomenon but a competition between avoidance and attraction, resolved differently by season, sex, traffic volume, road class, snow depth, and the presence or absence of predators.

This post reviews how that competition has been modelled. A recurring observation in methodological reviews of movement ecology is that the field’s apparent disagreement about whether moose avoid or prefer roads reflects, in large part, differences in what each model measures. A resource selection function estimates relative selection given a chosen availability set; a step selection function estimates the same thing but defines availability by the movement kernel; an integrated step selection function estimates selection and movement jointly; a continuous-time stochastic model estimates drift and diffusion fields and yields a stationary distribution; a hidden Markov model estimates behaviour-specific selection; and a collision-risk model estimates a hazard on road segments. These are not competing estimates of one number. They are estimates of different functionals, and the mathematics identifies which functional each model targets and under what assumptions it is identified.

Throughout, positions live in a domain and roads are a set that we treat as a union of curves,

with the distance-to-road field. The whole review can be read as a catalogue of the different ways , and its cousin the crossing event, enter a likelihood.

This post complements earlier posts on this blog: the ellipse method for bounding a path between fixes, the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model, and the general Fokker-Planck model. Where the continuous-time framework below overlaps those posts, the derivation is kept short and the reader is pointed back.

What is being estimated?

Before comparing models it is worth naming the estimands, because most disputes in the moose-road literature are disputes about which one is intended.

  1. Relative selection. The ratio of used to available density at a location, where is the intensity of use and is the intensity of availability. This is a dimensionless quantity, defined only up to a positive constant, and meaningful only relative to the availability measure (Manly et al. 1993; Boyce and McDonald 1999).
  2. The movement kernel. The distribution of a step, , as a function of step length and turning angle , possibly depending on habitat.
  3. Crossing intensity. The expected number of crossings of the road network per unit time,
  4. Collision hazard. The expected number of moose-vehicle collisions per unit time and unit road length, , on segment at time .

Frameworks 1–2 are selection models; 3–4 are exposure/risk models. The bridge between them is the flux of the animal across the road line, the quantity on which the exposure models and the selection models differ most sharply. The same crossing event is approached from the deterministic side in the ellipse-bounding method: given a maximum speed and two fixes, it determines which road crossings are even physically possible.

The observation layer comes first

Every model above is fitted to GPS telemetry, and GPS telemetry is not the position process. It is the position process composed with an error and missingness mechanism. Writing the truth as and the fixes as at times ,

where the error distribution is not homogeneous: it depends on canopy closure, terrain, collar orientation, and whether the animal is moving or bedded (Moen et al. 1996; D’Eon and Delparte 2005). Fix success is likewise selective. If indicates whether a scheduled fix succeeded, then varies with habitat, and ignoring it biases habitat selection estimates; the standard correction is to model fix success as a function of habitat and reweight, or to include it as a detection layer (Frair et al. 2004). Taken together, these studies establish a point that has become standard in the movement ecology literature: the telemetry device is itself a habitat-selective sampler (Moen et al. 1996; D’Eon and Delparte 2005; Frair et al. 2004).

Three consequences of this observation layer matter specifically for roads.

Attraction to the truth by measurement. Because has a kink (and zero set) on the roads themselves, additive error is not innocuous. For any ,

so fixes near a road are pushed systematically away from the road by roughly , while fixes far from a road can be pushed either way. If the estimated selection gradient is on while the true one is on , the discrepancy is classical attenuation plus a road-mediated contamination term, and its sign depends on the local density of animals at intermediate distances. In practice authors either discard fixes within a radius of the estimated error or use a spatial error model; the point is that the choice must be made explicitly.

False and missed crossings. Define the crossing event of a recorded step as

A true crossing can be missed if both endpoints are displaced to the same side, and a false crossing can appear if either endpoint is displaced across the road. The probability of a false crossing is therefore bounded below by

With location errors of tens of metres, moose that spend time within a road-effect zone of the same order are misclassified at non-negligible rates. For this reason, crossing counts are usually reported alongside a stated error model, and the ellipse method for bounding paths provides a hard, error-free check on which crossings are even possible.

Fix rate is a scale filter. A consequential observation-level choice is the time between fixes, . Let and be the probabilities that a used and an available step, respectively, cross a road during an interval of length . A step selection model can only detect a road effect through the contrast between these two probabilities, and the relevant contrast is on the log-odds scale,

Now let : both probabilities tend to zero, and the step never resolves the road. Let : both probabilities tend to one, and again the contrast vanishes. Information about road selection is concentrated at intermediate fix rates, where is bounded away from both and . Thurfjell, Ciuti and Boyce make exactly this argument with hypothetical moose: 15- and 30-minute fixes never cross the road and suggest pure avoidance, while 45- and 60-minute fixes produce steps that cut across it and can suggest preference (Thurfjell et al. 2014). Their example indicates how the scale of observation, rather than the biology, can drive the answer. Results of this kind should be read with the fix rate attached.

Resource selection functions: use versus availability

The oldest and still most common framework compares where an animal was used to what was available. Let and be the use and availability intensities. The selection function is

and in the exponential (log-linear) family

where is a vector of covariates, one of which is typically or a road-density covariate in a buffer. Availability is usually implemented as a sample of points drawn from the study area or from within each home range, and the model is fitted by logistic regression in a case-control design: used units as cases, available units as controls. Under that design the slope is consistently estimated even though the intercept is only identified up to the marginal case proportion (Manly et al. 1993; Boyce and McDonald 1999).

The relative nature of is a defining property of the framework rather than a technical nuisance: two researchers who define availability differently — one sampling uniformly over the study area, one sampling within a 95% minimum convex polygon per individual — are not estimating the same , and both are estimating something real. Johnson’s hierarchy codifies this (Johnson 1980): selection of a home range within the geographic range (second order), of patches within the home range (third order), of food items within patches (fourth order). Moose-road studies sit mostly at the second and third orders, and the covariate that means “avoidance” at one order is often a different object than the covariate that means “avoidance” at another.

Three refinements recur in the moose literature.

Functional responses. The coefficient on a road covariate is usually not constant across the population or the landscape. Writing for the road density at the home-range scale lets selection itself depend on the context in which the animal chooses, which is the functional response in habitat selection (Beest et al. 2015). Beyer and colleagues found exactly this threshold behaviour in moose: avoidance of roads strengthens above a road-density threshold, and the response differs by season and time of day (Beyer et al. 2013). Finnegan and colleagues found functional responses to seismic lines and pipelines but, at the population level, indifference to roads, with individual variation doing the work (Finnegan et al. 2023).

Individual variation. Selection coefficients vary among individuals. A random-effects specification,

with the individual deviation vector, is the mixed conditional-logistic model developed for exactly these matched use-availability designs (Duchesne et al. 2010). The two-stage alternative — fit each animal separately, then analyse the coefficient estimates — is simpler and gives the same population mean with a between-individual variance estimate (Gillies et al. 2011). The distinction matters for roads because the coefficient of interest is often a variance in road avoidance, not just its mean: some moose in a herd of collared animals are habitual road users and some are not.

Probability versus relative intensity. If one wants the actual probability that an available unit is used rather than a ratio, the exponential model must be normalized,

This is the resource selection probability function, and unlike it is an absolute quantity, but it requires a correctly normalized availability measure over a bounded domain (Manly et al. 1993). Most published moose-road “RSFs” are relative selection functions, and the difference explains why their coefficients cannot be compared across studies with different availability domains.

Step selection: making availability the movement kernel

The critique of use-availability RSFs is that a uniform availability set is not what the animal could have reached. A moose cannot materialize on the far side of a lake or beyond a ridge in the next hour. Step selection functions replace the abstract availability set with the reachable set implied by the observed movement, and in doing so they make the movement kernel part of the model (Fortin et al. 2005).

Let be the current location and write a step by its polar coordinates

The step-selection model assumes that the density of a used step is proportional to a selection weight times a movement kernel,

where typically is a gamma or exponential density on step length and a von Mises density on turning angle,

with the modified Bessel function. Availability is generated by sampling from the same kernel around each observed start point, and the model is fitted by conditional logistic regression: for each used step and available steps ,

Because the movement kernel is common to the numerator and every denominator term, it cancels: the conditional likelihood identifies without committing to the movement parameters. This cancellation is what makes the method attractive, and also the source of its main caveat. The appealing part is that SSF coefficients have a clean interpretation as log relative selection, exactly as in the RSF, but with availability defined by movement. The caveat is that the cancellation is only valid if the availability kernel used to sample is the true movement kernel, or at least proportional to it on the support that matters. Under misspecification the cancelled factor does not cancel and is biased; Forester, Im and Rathouz showed this in simulation and showed that including step length (and turning angle) as covariates absorbs much of the misspecification, because the movement attributes then enter the linear predictor explicitly (Forester et al. 2009).

There is an equivalent and, for our purposes, more revealing way to write the same model. The used-step process is an inhomogeneous Poisson point process on the step space with intensity

conditioned on one point per stratum. In this form the SSF is the discrete-time cousin of a continuous-time selection model, and the two can be made to agree at fine temporal resolution. It is also the form in which the road covariate question becomes sharp.

Where is the road covariate measured? This is the point on which moose-road SSFs most often differ, and it is not a cosmetic choice. A linear feature can enter at the step’s endpoint, ; along the path, ; or through a buffer around the path. Endpoints capture being near a road; path integrals capture crossing it. Thurfjell and colleagues make the argument geometrically: if a wolf walks along a road but the mapped road is a vector without width, no endpoint will ever land exactly on the road, and endpoint measurement underestimates selection for linear features; if instead a road is avoided, only path- or buffer-based covariates register the crossing (Thurfjell et al. 2014). For moose, whose response to roads can change sign depending on whether the animal is lingering or traversing, this covariate definition can determine the sign of the estimated effect. The SSF literature can therefore report avoidance and attraction for the same animal, depending on whether the covariate of interest is a distance at the endpoint or an integral along the step.

Relative step selection strength. Because is exponential, the effect size for comparing two steps is a log ratio,

the relative selection strength, which can be plotted against one covariate while holding the rest fixed (Avgar et al. 2017). Prokopenko, Boyce and Avgar use precisely this device for elk responding to roads, giving curves of relative selection as a function of distance to road and time of day, and showing that the same coefficient can encode avoidance at one hour and neutrality at another (Prokopenko et al. 2016).

Integrated step selection: estimating movement and selection together

The SSF’s movement kernel cancels, which is convenient for inference about but leaves the model unable to predict movement. The integrated step selection function (iSSF, also iSSA) estimates both the selection and movement components in one conditional likelihood (Avgar et al. 2016). The used-step density is

and, crucially, the movement parameters and are treated as functions of habitat and estimated jointly with , rather than being fixed by the sampling procedure. In the simplest case the linear predictor becomes

which shows that an iSSF is an SSF with the movement terms moved inside the linear predictor. The parameter is a mean step length (a speed), and a directional persistence; estimating them as functions of answers a biologically different question from the RSF, namely whether moose move faster (or more directionally) near roads. That is the “haste” hypothesis — animals traversing a risky neighbourhood at speed rather than lingering — and it is not testable with a plain RSF.

The payoff of integrating movement is predictive. Once , and are known, the model is a mechanistic, habitat-dependent random walk with redistribution kernel

and the stationary utilization distribution is the solution of the balance equation

This is an eigenvalue problem for the chain, and solving it by simulation is the standard “scaling up” from step decisions to space use (Avgar et al. 2016; Potts and Börger 2023). The stationary distribution turns out to have the same functional form as an RSF weight, which is the deep reason the two families keep agreeing empirically despite being fitted to different data (Moorcroft and Barnett 2008; Potts and Schlägel 2020). For managers, the practical consequence is that an iSSF fitted to moose steps can be used to simulate the effect of a new road or a fence in silico, which an RSF cannot do without additional assumptions.

Continuous time: from step models to diffusion and Fokker-Planck

The discrete-time step models are approximations to a continuous process, and writing the continuous process explicitly buys a set of tools — boundary conditions, flux, stationary solutions — that the discrete models lack. The starting point is the Ito stochastic differential equation for position,

whose density obeys the Fokker-Planck equation

This framework is developed in detail in the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and general Fokker-Planck posts, including the OU reduction, the Boltzmann equilibrium for gradient drifts , and nonlocal interaction terms. What matters here is the menu of ways to represent a road.

Roads as a drift field (taxis). Let be an environmental cue, for instance (so that smaller distance to road means larger cue) or a traffic-weighted density. The class of diffusion-taxis models adds a directed drift along the cue,

with attracting and repelling. Potts and Schlägel showed that step selection analysis at fine temporal resolution parametrizes exactly this class, and that the steady-state utilization distribution has the same closed form as a resource selection function (Potts and Schlägel 2020). This is the formal bridge between the movement-first and selection-first literatures: an RSF is (under regularity) the long-run distribution of a taxis process, and the coefficients are related by in the linear case. It also clarifies what a road coefficient means: it is a drift, not a preference, and it is only interpretable as a stationary preference if the process is ergodic and the domain bounded, which a real moose range with fences, highways and seasonal migration is not guaranteed to be.

Roads as a boundary. The alternative is to treat a road as a semi-permeable line and impose a boundary condition on the probability current . A fully avoiding moose has a no-flux condition on ,

a crossing moose has a partial-flux or radiative condition, and a lethal crossing can be represented by a sink concentrated on , removing the tiny probability mass that enters the carriageway. These are exactly the barrier and sink devices built into the general Fokker-Planck model, and they are the natural home for the barrier aspect of roads, which most step-based studies handle only implicitly through availability. A continuous-time formulation also separates observation error from process: the correlated random walk for the velocity,

fitted to noisy fixes as a continuous-time correlated random walk, is the standard way to estimate movement parameters from error-contaminated telemetry without first cleaning the tracks (Johnson et al. 2008). The moose-specific case is instructive: movement rates, and not merely positions, respond to roads, and a process model estimates rates directly.

Hidden states: behaviour changes the road response

A moose that is bedded, browsing, or travelling is, for modelling purposes, three different animals. Hidden Markov models make this explicit. Let be a latent behavioural state following a Markov chain with generator and transition matrix , and let the observation (a step, or activity-sensor reading) have state-specific density . The likelihood is computed by the forward recursion

and the resulting decoded states are the familiar “resting / foraging / travelling” tracks (Patterson et al. 2009; Michelot et al. 2016). State-space models do the same job in a Bayesian framework with process and observation error separated (Jonsen et al. 2005).

For roads the payoff is state-dependent selection. Allowing the road coefficient to differ by state,

tests the specific hypothesis that moose avoid roads while resting but use them as travel corridors while moving — a pattern that a single coefficient averages away. Combining an HMM with an integrated step-selection analysis is now standard, and has been applied directly to moose, linking behaviour-dependent selection to forage maps (Graf et al. 2026). The methodological cost is identifiability: with states, road coefficients, and a transition matrix, a single track can support many explanations, and weakly informative priors or strong ecological constraints are needed.

Crossings and collisions: exposure and hazard

Selection models estimate where moose prefer to be. Collision models estimate where and when moose die. The bridge is the crossing process, and it is where the moose-road literature splits most sharply.

The rate at which moose cross a road line is a flux. For the diffusion process above, the expected number of crossings of a small road element of normal per unit time is the outward normal component of the probability current integrated over the road,

This quantity is not the same as selection for or against , and the difference is the reason two studies can report both avoidance and high crossing rates. An animal can avoid roads for long periods and still cross them when it must, and the crossing flux is controlled by the drift toward and geometry of the road, by snow that funnels movement, and by the arrangement of habitat on either side. Dussault and colleagues modelled crossing probability explicitly from moose telemetry and found movement rates elevated along highways — moose move faster near roads, consistent with haste rather than attraction (Dussault et al. 2007). Laurian and colleagues described the behavioural profile of moose relative to a road network, including the elevated movement rates that accompany crossings (Laurian et al. 2008).

The hazard side multiplies crossing exposure by traffic. For a road segment, a first-order model is

where is vehicle flow and the probability that a crossing co-occurs with a vehicle within the reaction window, which decreases with animal speed and increases with traffic speed and flow. Empirically, collision risk rises with traffic volume up to a peak and then plateaus, and it rises with speed limit (Danks and Porter 2010). The winter pattern is the clearest demonstration that movement and traffic must be modelled together: across the Arctic-boreal region, moose migrated to lower elevations as snow deepened, into shallower snow and higher road density, and collisions were 2.4 to 5.7 times more frequent in December–February than in early summer, with most occurring after dark (Cunningham et al. 2022). Neither a movement model alone nor a traffic model alone reproduces that.

Two modelling designs dominate the applied collision literature, and both are easy to misread.

The case-control design at collision sites compares the landscape at reported collisions to random points along the same roads, giving a logistic model of the odds of collision given site covariates (Danks and Porter 2010; Wattles et al. 2018). Its limitation is that the denominator is a road-length sample, not an animal-exposure sample, so a strong “selection” for a roadside feature may reflect where moose cross rather than where they die, and a road with no reported collisions may simply have low traffic or low moose density. The remedy, pioneered for moose in Massachusetts, is to incorporate the road-crossing process estimated from telemetry as an offset or a component of the risk model, so that exposure and lethality are separated (Zeller et al. 2018). This is the empirical realization of the flux decomposition above.

The movement-informed design fits collision probability as a function of the phase of the animal’s movement (crossing versus not) and the environment, and has been used to show that collisions cluster where and when moose cross, not merely where they live (Laliberté and St-Laurent 2020).

Comparing the frameworks

The table below summarizes the frameworks as they appear in the literature. The “road enters as” column is the key: the frameworks estimate different functionals of the path rather than disagreeing about moose per se.

Framework Estimand Availability / baseline Road enters as Observation error Chief bias Moose-road exemplars
Use-availability RSF relative selection fixed domain (home range or study area) endpoint covariate or density usually ignored arbitrary availability; scale dependence Beyer et al. (2013); Finnegan et al. (2023)
SSF relative selection at the step scale movement kernel endpoint or path integral mostly ignored kernel misspecification; fix-rate sensitivity Fortin et al. (2005); Prokopenko et al. (2016)
iSSF / iSSA joint selection and movement movement kernel, estimated movement parameters and can be built in confounding movement with selection Avgar et al. (2016); Graf et al. (2026)
Diffusion-taxis / Fokker-Planck drift, diffusion, stationary UD mechanistic process drift field or boundary condition process vs. error separable hard to fit; strong structural assumptions Moorcroft and Barnett (2008); Potts and Schlägel (2020); Johnson et al. (2008)
HMM / state-space state-specific selection and transition state-specific kernels state-dependent explicit identifiability; state number Patterson et al. (2009); Michelot et al. (2016); Jonsen et al. (2005)
Crossing-flux expected crossings exposure process flux across the line error inflates false crossings geometry and error Dussault et al. (2007); Laurian et al. (2008)
Collision hazard / case-control collision rate per road length road-length sample site covariates + exposure offset under-reporting denominator, exposure, reporting Danks and Porter (2010); Wattles et al. (2018); Zeller et al. (2018); Laliberté and St-Laurent (2020)

Reading down the “road enters as” column, the apparent contradictions of the moose literature can be read as differences in estimand. Studies that measure endpoint distance tend to find avoidance or indifference; studies that measure movement rate find haste near roads; studies that measure crossing or collision find elevated hazard near roads at certain times. These are consistent statements about one animal.

What the moose literature reports

With the estimands pinned down, the empirical picture reported in the literature is fairly coherent, and its variations are systematic rather than contradictory.

Avoidance is the population-level default in predator-rich, traffic-heavy landscapes. Moose avoid areas close to roads throughout the year in Quebec, with higher movement rates near roads and larger home ranges where road density is higher, and with the aversion stronger in winter (Laurian et al. 2008; Gagnon et al. 2024). Avoidance strengthens non-linearly with road density, with thresholds that differ by season and diel phase (Beyer et al. 2013). Beyer’s Alberta moose were more selective at finer scales, which is the expected signature of a functional response.

Attraction appears where a resource is concentrated at the roadside. In eastern Poland, moose preferred roads at night in winter, plausibly for sodium from de-icing salt and for thinner snow on ploughed verges (Borowik et al. 2024). Roadside mineral licks in British Columbia attract moose, with obvious collision consequences (Huxter et al. 2024). The attraction is not a contradiction of avoidance; it is a seasonal, resource-driven taxis superimposed on a chronic risk-avoidance drift.

The sign of the road effect is often undetectable at the population mean. In the Alberta foothills, moose were indifferent to roads at the population level while responding to seismic lines and pipelines, with the individual variation carrying the signal (Finnegan et al. 2023). This is exactly the situation in which a random-effects selection model is required, and in which a mean-only RSF reports a null that hides two well-separated behaviours.

Movement rate, not preference, may be the robust road response. The most reproducible effect across studies is that moose move faster near roads — the haste response — whereas the sign of the positional preference is study-specific (Dussault et al. 2007; Laurian et al. 2008; Gagnon et al. 2024). This pattern motivates the use of integrated and continuous-time models, which estimate movement parameters directly, over pure selection models.

Collision risk is an exposure problem, not a preference problem. The winter migration result (Cunningham et al. 2022) and the Massachusetts crossing-exposure model (Zeller et al. 2018) both show that the collision rate is governed by where movement takes animals and when traffic is present, more than by any stable preference for roadsides. Case-control studies that ignore exposure will systematically attribute to preference what belongs to flux.

Roads are barriers whose permeability is scale-dependent. At very fine temporal resolution a road is a line that steps rarely cross, so a step model sees avoidance; at coarse resolution it is a feature every step crosses, so the model sees nothing. The permeability that matters ecologically — do moose cross, how often, and at what cost — is a property of the movement process on the scale of the reaction window, and continuous-time and hidden-state models are the frameworks that represent this permeability explicitly.

Open problems

Four problems cut across all the frameworks, and they are widely discussed in the methodological literature as issues of inference rather than of biology.

Availability is doing the work. In every selection model the road coefficient is defined relative to an availability measure, and the choice of that measure — study area versus home range versus step kernel versus diffusion process — changes the estimate. The unification result, that the stationary distribution of a diffusion-taxis process has the form of an RSF and can be parametrized by step selection analysis, tells us the frameworks are connected (Potts and Schlägel 2020; Moorcroft and Barnett 2008; Potts and Börger 2023), but it also means that reporting a road coefficient without its availability convention is reporting an incomplete quantity. Methodological reviews therefore call for reporting the availability kernel or domain alongside every road coefficient, as the iSSF literature now does for movement parameters.

Scale is a covariate choice, not a nuisance. Fix rate, buffer radius, and the width of the road-effect zone are all scale choices, and Thurfjell’s argument shows the road response can flip sign across them (Thurfjell et al. 2014). A multi-scale or continuous-scale treatment — fitting selection as a function of the scale itself, or using the fix-rate sensitivity analysis they recommend — is the exception rather than the rule in the moose literature.

Observation error is still weakly handled. Given a location error comparable to the width of the road-effect zone, false crossings and attenuated gradients are first-order effects, not second-order ones (Moen et al. 1996; D’Eon and Delparte 2005; Frair et al. 2004). Yet the majority of moose-road studies fit selection at the raw fixes, and collision studies rarely propagate telemetry error into the crossing exposure that drives the hazard. Continuous-time state-space models that estimate movement and error jointly (Johnson et al. 2008; Jonsen et al. 2005) provide a principled treatment of this error and are less common in the moose-road literature.

Causality. Almost all of the evidence is observational, and traffic, road density, predators, forage, snow and hunting are confounded at the landscape scale. The models are good at describing the joint distribution of movement and roads and poor at isolating the effect of a change in the road environment. Two directions have been proposed: manipulating traffic (closures, seasonal speed limits) and measuring the response, and using the mechanistic models to generate testable counterfactual predictions. The iSSF and diffusion-taxis models are the members of this family that make falsifiable out-of-sample predictions about new road configurations, which is what a mitigation appraisal requires.

Conclusion

Moose movement in relation to roads is a well-posed problem only once the estimand is stated. Relative selection, movement rate, crossing flux, and collision hazard are four different functionals of the same trajectory, and the modelling frameworks of the literature — resource selection functions, step selection functions, integrated step selection, continuous-time diffusion and Fokker-Planck models, hidden Markov and state-space models, and collision hazard models — are estimators of those functionals under different assumptions about availability, scale, and observation error. The step selection family is the workhorse because it makes availability a movement kernel and estimates selection at the scale at which moose actually decide; the integrated form adds the ability to predict movement and hence to simulate interventions; the continuous-time diffusion-taxis formulation supplies the boundary conditions, flux, and stationary solutions needed to connect selection to exposure; and the collision models supply the denominator that turns movement into risk. The empirical record is less contradictory than it appears: moose avoid the chronic risks of roads, are drawn to roadside resources in specific seasons, traverse roads at speed when they cross, and die where those crossings coincide with traffic and darkness. The methodological literature suggests that further progress lies less in new model families than in using the connections between them — availability made explicit, scale treated as a modelled quantity, observation error propagated, and the mechanistic models used to generate testable counterfactual predictions.

item.title: Indivisible Stochastic Processes and the Stochastic–Quantum Correspondence
item.dc:creator: Galen Seilis
item.description:
Introduction

The standard formulation of quantum theory rests on the Dirac–von Neumann axioms: states are vectors (or density matrices) in a Hilbert space, observables are self-adjoint operators, isolated systems evolve by a unitary operator (equivalently, by the Schrödinger equation), and measurement outcomes are governed by the Born rule (Dirac 1930; Neumann 1932). These axioms are empirically magnificent but conceptually divided: they treat “measurement” as an unexplained primitive and offer no account of what is happening in an experiment before a measurement is complete.

In a series of recent papers, Jacob Barandes has argued that a quantum system can instead be understood as a perfectly ordinary stochastic process unfolding in an old-fashioned configuration space, governed by probabilistic laws that are non-Markovian in a specific and previously unstudied sense. The central object is the indivisible stochastic process, and the central result is the stochastic–quantum correspondence (Barandes 2025b, 2025a):

Indivisible stochastic processes generically exhibit all the hallmark empirical features of quantum systems, including interference, decoherence, entanglement, and noncommutative observables, and a quantum system evolving unitarily can be understood as an indivisible stochastic process in disguise.

The payoff is a reformulation in which the Hilbert space and its ingredients—wave functions, state vectors, and Hamiltonians—are derived mathematical appurtenances rather than axioms, and in which the “measurement problem” is dissolved rather than solved.

The purpose of this post is to give a thorough and self-contained account. Because the correspondence draws simultaneously on probability theory, the theory of stochastic processes, and quantum mechanics, I begin by laying out the prerequisites in each of those areas. I then give the formal definition of an indivisible stochastic process, the precise sense in which it fails to be Markovian, the dictionary that connects it to a Hilbert space, the Kraus and Stinespring machinery that yields unitary evolution, and finally the stochastic–quantum theorem itself. Throughout, definitions, lemmas, propositions, and theorems are stated formally and, where instructive, proved.

This is a long post. A reader who wants the conceptual through-line rather than the full machinery may read the introduction to each part and the statements of the main results, and treat the proofs and technical definitions as a reference.

This post is purely expository. Every definition, result, interpretation, and argument below is due to Jacob Barandes and the other authors cited; I am reporting, organizing, and explaining their work, not proposing any new ideas of my own. The choice of material, the exposition, and any errors of presentation are mine, but the substance is theirs. Readers interested in the original development should consult the cited primary sources.

Roadmap

  • Part I collects prerequisites: probability theory and conditional probability; the theory of stochastic processes (Kolmogorov towers, Chapman–Kolmogorov, Markovianity, divisibility, stochastic matrices); and quantum mechanics (Hilbert spaces, density matrices, the Born rule, unitary dynamics, projection-valued measures, completely positive maps, and the Stinespring dilation theorem).
  • Part II defines indivisible stochastic processes, explains divisibility and its failure, and states the axioms of indivisible quantum theory.
  • Part III develops the stochastic–quantum correspondence: the time-evolution operator, Schur–Hadamard gauge freedom, the dictionary, the Hilbert-space representation, Kraus decompositions, dilations, and the stochastic–quantum theorem.
  • Part IV discusses gauge invariance, dynamical symmetries, dilations, the complex numbers, and the interpretational consequences for measurement, hidden variables, Bell’s theorem, and causation.

1.2 Conditional probability and the law of total probability

Definition 4 (Conditional probability). For events with , the conditional probability of given is

Theorem 5 (Law of total probability). Let be a finite or countable partition of with for all . Then for any event ,

1.3 Independence

2. Stochastic Processes

2.1 Kolmogorov towers and transition probabilities

Textbook treatments (Kolmogorov 1933; Doob 1953; Ross 1995) define a stochastic process as a family of random variables indexed by time, together with a probability distribution, and add the specification of a dynamical law.

Definition 8 (Configuration space). The configuration space of a stochastic process is a fixed set whose elements are the possible configurations of the system.

Definition 8a (Standalone probability distribution). A standalone probability distribution is a time-dependent function giving the probability (or probability density) that the system is in configuration at time , satisfying

Definition 8b (Algebra of random variables). The algebra of random variables of a stochastic process with configuration space is the collection of time-dependent maps , with values , whose expectation is

Definition 8c (Stochastic process). A stochastic process is the data of a configuration space (Definition 8), a standalone probability distribution (Definition 8a), and an algebra of random variables (Definition 8b).

The configuration space is a fixed ingredient of the model; the standalone distribution is contingent, in that it can differ from run to run.

Definition 9 (Transition probability). A transition probability of a stochastic process is a conditional probability of the form , the probability that the system is in configuration at time given that it was in configurations at the earlier times .

Definition 9a (Kolmogorov tower). The Kolmogorov tower of a general stochastic process is the infinite hierarchy of transition probabilities (Definition 9) where .

Definition 9b (Target time). In a transition probability , the time on the left of the bar is the target time.

Definition 9c (Conditioning times). In a transition probability , the times on the right of the bar are the conditioning times. The bar is read “given” and the semicolon “and.”

Definition 10 (Joint probabilities). The joint probability of configurations at two times is the product of the transition probability and the standalone distribution:

Definition 10b (Chapman–Kolmogorov equations). The transition probabilities must satisfy the marginalization consistency conditions for every time index : summing over the intermediate configuration reproduces the joint probability with that time omitted.

2.2 Markovianity and divisibility

Definition 11 (Markov property). A stochastic process is Markovian if every second- and higher-order transition probability equals the corresponding first-order transition probability for the latest conditioning time, i.e. The latest conditioning time then “screens off” all earlier times.

Definition 11b (Non-Markovian process). A stochastic process is non-Markovian if it does not satisfy Definition 11: some higher-order transition probability fails to reduce to the corresponding first-order one.

Definition 11c (Conditional independence). Events and are conditionally independent given an event (with ) if (Definition 4). The Markov property (Definition 11) says the present conditionally separates the past from the future.

The screening-off property of Definition 11 is exactly the conditional independence familiar from graphical models (Pearl 2009; Spirtes et al. 2001): the present renders the past and future independent.

Definition 12 (Transition matrix). For a stochastic process, the transition matrix is the matrix whose -th row, -th column entry is the first-order transition probability

Proposition 13 (Column stochasticity). Every transition matrix is a (column) stochastic matrix:

Proof. Non-negativity and column normalization are the defining properties of conditional probabilities, together with the normalization of the standalone distribution.

Definition 14 (Divisibility). A stochastic process is divisible over an interval if, for any intermediate time between and , its transition matrices factorize as

Proposition 15 (Markovianity implies divisibility). A Markovian process is divisible.

Proof. With the Markov property (Definition 11) and the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations (Definition 10b), one shows that second-order transition probabilities compose, so that the probability at time is obtained by summing over all intermediate configurations. In matrix form this is precisely (13).

The contrapositive of Proposition 15 is the remark that will drive the whole subject: indivisibility entails non-Markovianity.

Definition 16 (Trivialization of a Kolmogorov tower). A Kolmogorov tower (Definition 9a) trivializes after orders if, for every , each -th-order transition probability equals the corresponding first-order transition probability for the latest conditioning time.

Definition 16a (th-order non-Markovian process). A non-Markovian process (Definition 11b) is th-order non-Markovian if its Kolmogorov tower trivializes (Definition 16) after orders for some finite integer . A Markov process is the case . Newtonian mechanics, viewed deterministically, is second-order non-Markovian, because Newton’s second law is a second-order differential equation.

Example 17 (Discrete-time homogeneous Markov chain). On a finite time scale , a homogeneous chain (Definition 16c) satisfies for a time-independent stochastic matrix . This is a unistochastic process when is a permutation matrix (see §13 and Example 40).

Definition 16b (Markov chain). A Markov chain is a Markovian (Definition 11) stochastic process with discrete configuration space; its law is determined by its first-order transition probabilities (Definition 12).

Definition 16c (Time homogeneity). A stochastic process is time-homogeneous if its transition matrices depend only on the time difference, ; otherwise it is time-inhomogeneous.

2.3 Stochastic and permutation matrices

Definition 18a (Column stochastic matrix). An matrix with non-negative real entries is column stochastic if for every column , .

Definition 18b (Doubly stochastic/bistochastic matrix). A matrix is doubly stochastic (or bistochastic) if it is column stochastic and row stochastic in the sense that for every row , (equivalently both row and column sums are 1).

Definition 18c (Permutation). A permutation of a finite set is a bijection (Definition S2f) . The permutations of form a group (Definition LA0) under composition (Definition S2g).

Definition 19 (Permutation matrix). A permutation matrix is a matrix of s and s with exactly one in each row and in each column. Every permutation matrix is doubly stochastic (Definition 18b) and orthogonal (Definition LA10) (and therefore unitary, Definition 30b).

Lemma 20 (Permutation lemma). Let and be matrices with non-negative entries and . Then (and hence ) is a permutation matrix.

Proof. The first row of must be orthogonal (Definition LA9) to each of the second through -th columns of . Since is invertible, its columns are linearly independent, so the first row of is orthogonal to an -dimensional subspace. Because all entries of and are non-negative, the only way this orthogonality can hold is if exactly one entry of the first row of is nonzero, and the corresponding entries in the other columns of vanish. Repeating for each row of shows every row has a single nonzero entry; if is stochastic, that entry is . Hence is a permutation matrix, and since the inverse of a permutation matrix is again a permutation matrix, is too.

This lemma appears, with this proof, in (Barandes 2025a, footnote 7). Its consequence is the non-divisibility of indivisible processes: the naive intermediate matrix is generally not stochastic, and may even have negative entries.

Definition 21 (Pseudo-stochastic matrix). A matrix is pseudo-stochastic if each of its columns sums to but its entries are real (or complex in generalizations) and need not be non-negative (Chruściński et al. 2015). Pseudo-stochastic matrices form a semigroup (Definition 21a) and, unlike stochastic matrices, allow affine combinations (Definition 21c) beyond non-negative convex combinations (Definition 21b), and carry a Lie-group structure (Definition 21d).

Definition 21a (Semigroup). A semigroup is a set equipped with an associative binary operation; unlike a group (Definition LA0) it need not possess an identity or inverses.

Definition 21b (Convex combination). A convex combination of points in a real vector space is with and .

Definition 21c (Affine combination). An affine combination is with , where the coefficients are allowed to be negative.

Definition 21d (Lie group). A Lie group is a group (Definition LA0) that is also a smooth (differentiable) manifold, with group multiplication and inversion smooth as maps.

3. Prerequisites from Quantum Mechanics

3.1 The Dirac–von Neumann axioms

Axiom 22 (Dirac–von Neumann, schematic). A quantum system is described by the following.

The famous measurement problem is the ambiguity, internal to this axiom set, over which physical processes count as “measurements.” The category problem is the separate difficulty of accounting for the far larger class of non-measurement events happening in the world (Barandes 2025a).

Part II: Indivisible Stochastic Processes

4. Definition and Immediate Properties

The idea of an indivisible stochastic process first appeared in passing in a 2021 review of quantum non-Markovianity (Milz and Modi 2021, fig. 6), with rudimentary forms traceable to work on open quantum systems (Wolf and Cirac 2008). Barandes builds them into a complete framework (Barandes 2025b).

Definition 33 (Indivisible stochastic process). An indivisible stochastic process is a tuple consisting of:

  1. a configuration space , a fixed set of possible configurations;
  2. a set of target times ;
  3. a set of conditioning times (or division events) , containing an initial time ;
  4. a transition map with entries defined only for conditioning times , satisfying the normalization condition
  5. a probability distribution , satisfying the normalization condition and the law of total probability
  6. an algebra of random variables : the maps .

The transition map is also required to satisfy the trivialization condition for every , and the continuity condition .

Remark 34 (What is and is not assumed). Three features distinguish this definition from a textbook stochastic process.

  • Only first-order laws. The nomological content is a single first-order transition map, not an infinite Kolmogorov tower. The law of total probability (19) is the only Chapman–Kolmogorov equation available.
  • Division events are sparse and system-centric. Transition probabilities are not assumed to exist for every conditioning time, only for division events. Division events are not global properties of the universe; they are features of a given subsystem and may be generated to excellent approximation through interactions (Barandes 2025a).
  • No assumption that . The target time may lie before the conditioning time, so logical time-reversal invariance is not violated fundamentally.

5. Divisibility and Its Failure

Proposition 35 (Linearity). The law of total probability (19) is linear in the standalone distribution: .

Proof. Immediate from (19) written in matrix-vector form.

This linearity is the seed of the linearity of quantum time evolution (Barandes 2025a).

Proposition 36 (Indivisibility entails non-Markovianity). An indivisible stochastic process is generically not divisible, and therefore generically not Markovian.

Proof. Suppose one attempts to define an intermediate transition matrix between and through an intermediate time : By construction . But by Lemma 20, is a stochastic matrix only if both factors are permutation matrices. In general it is pseudo-stochastic (Definition 21), with negative entries, and is not a legitimate transition matrix. Hence the dynamics do not divide at . By the contrapositive of Proposition 15, the process is non-Markovian.

The failure of divisibility is therefore not the familiar failure of Markovianity as memory in the sense of needing higher-order conditionals. An indivisible process has vastly less nomological structure than a textbook non-Markovian process, yet is still non-Markovian, because it does not divide at all.

Remark 37 (Non-Markovian realizers). Given only the sparse ingredients of Definition 33, there generically exists a large or infinite family of complete Kolmogorov towers consistent with them. Any such tower that matches the system’s statistics is called a non-Markovian realizer; an indivisible stochastic process encompasses an equivalence class of them. Only the minimalist ingredients are connected to empirical predictions, so the particular realizer is contingent, potentially unknowable, and arguably meaningless (Barandes 2025a).

7. Axioms of Indivisible Quantum Theory

The reformulation replaces the Dirac–von Neumann axioms with a smaller, more transparent set (Barandes 2025a).

Axiom 41 (Kinematical axiom). For each model, one selects an appropriate configuration space, whose members are the possible configurations of the system, treated as elementary. The configuration space is a fixed feature of the model.

Axiom 42 (Dynamical axiom). For arbitrary target times and for conditioning times that are division events, the dynamical laws consist of transition probabilities . Division events may arise intrinsically or through interactions; the transition probabilities are fixed features of the model.

Axiom 43 (Epistemic axiom). The system has a time-dependent standalone probability distribution, connected across times by the transition probabilities. It is contingent, varying between runs.

The kinematical and epistemic axioms are essentially classical; the distinctively non-classical ingredient is the dynamical axiom, which replaces Markovian differential equations with a sparse set of indivisible transition probabilities. The configurations play the role historically assigned to “hidden variables,” but they are not hidden: they are exactly what one sees in experiments, and they replace wave functions as the ontological content (Barandes 2025a).

Corollary 63. To study the class of indivisible stochastic processes, it suffices to study the subclass of unistochastic processes. Every indivisible stochastic process corresponds to a unitarily evolving quantum system, and unitarily evolving quantum systems represent the most general way to model a system with stochastic dynamical laws (Barandes 2023).

Corollary 64 (The correspondence is bidirectional). Reading the dictionary in the other direction, any quantum system can be modeled as an indivisible stochastic process. One thereby obtains the stochastic–quantum correspondence between indivisible stochastic processes and quantum systems (Barandes 2025b).

The correspondence is many-to-one in both directions, exactly as the correspondence between Newtonian systems and Hamiltonian mechanics: a given indivisible stochastic process admits infinitely many Hilbert-space representations, and a given Hilbert-space system represents infinitely many qualitatively different indivisible stochastic processes (one per choice of orthonormal basis serving as a configuration space) (Barandes 2025b).

Part IV: Further Implications

13. Hamiltonian Dynamics and the Emergence of the Schrödinger Equation

If the unitary time-evolution operator is differentiable in , define the Hamiltonian

Proposition 66. The density matrix satisfies the von Neumann equation, a rank-one state vector satisfies the Schrödinger equation, expectation values satisfy the Ehrenfest equation, and Heisenberg-picture operators satisfy the Heisenberg equation of motion:

Thus the Schrödinger equation is derived, not postulated, from an indivisible stochastic process with a differentiable unistochastic transition matrix. The conditions of linearity and probability conservation alone are insufficient to pick out unitarity—CPTP maps such as the bit-flip channel are linear and probability-conserving without being unitary—so the derivation of unitarity is a substantive result (Barandes 2025a).

14. Gauge Invariance and Dynamical Symmetries

14.1 Foldy–Wouthuysen gauge transformations

Proposition 67 (Second gauge invariance). Let be a time-dependent unitary matrix. The transformation leaves the probabilities, expectation values, and the transition matrix unchanged (Barandes 2025b).

This is a gauge invariance first written down for the Dirac equation by Foldy and Wouthuysen (Foldy and Wouthuysen 1950). If is time-independent it is a change of orthonormal basis; if it depends on time it is a local-in-time unitary transformation of each Hilbert-space fiber. Under it, when is unitary, the Hamiltonian transforms as a non-Abelian gauge potential: Choosing makes —which is precisely the Heisenberg picture. Consequently the Hamiltonian is not a gauge-invariant observable, and the familiar Hilbert-space ingredients are highly gauge-dependent; one may reasonably be skeptical of assigning them direct ontological meaning (Barandes 2025b).

15. Dilations, Spin, and the Complex Numbers

Proposition 70 (Dilation as a free enlargement). For any integer , the Hilbert-space formulation can be enlarged without changing the process by where is a PVM on an internal space of dimension . The dictionary is unchanged after a partial trace over .

Dilations provide a larger “canvas” for designing transition matrices and can make new dilation-emergeables—such as intrinsic spin—manifest. Representing spin this way requires dilating the Hilbert space to dimensions and introducing a -dimensional representation of for the internal space, so the underlying indivisible stochastic process involves no preferred direction (Barandes 2025b).

Remark 71 (Why the complex numbers appear). Unistochastic matrices are generally not orthostochastic, so if the transition matrix is already unistochastic there is no guarantee that its unitary square root can be taken real orthogonal. The correspondence therefore implies that, to represent the most general indivisible stochastic processes, the complex numbers are an important structural feature of quantum theory (Barandes 2023). One is always free to choose real, in which case the dilated is real orthogonal; and one can even double the dimension to represent the imaginary unit by a real matrix (Myrheim 1999) and the complex-conjugation operator by (Stueckelberg 1960). But even so, the algebraic structure of the complex numbers—and with it the spectral theorem, eigenvectors, anti-unitary operators, self-adjoint Hamiltonians, and the Schrödinger equation—becomes hard to avoid. These ideas are developed further in the deflationary account of (Barandes 2026).

16. Interpretation: Measurement, Hidden Variables, Locality, and Causation

The measurement and category problems. In the indivisible picture, a measurement is just another stochastic interaction, modeled as one additional part of a larger stochastic process. When a measuring device is so modeled, it ends up in one of its possible outcome configurations with the standard Born-rule probability, whether the observable was a beable or an emergeable (Barandes 2025b). This dissolves the measurement problem—there is no special “collapse” process, only ordinary stochastic dynamics—and addresses the category problem, since ordinary non-measurement events are the norm rather than the exception.

Comparison with earlier stochastic reformulations. Previous attempts to reformulate quantum theory stochastically—Bopp, Fényes, and Nelson’s stochastic mechanics (Nelson 1966), and later work (Aaronson 2005)—assumed Markovian laws and were thus limited. Spontaneous-collapse theories instead treat the wave function as primary and literally collapsing (Ghirardi et al. 1986; Bassi and Ghirardi 2003). Indivisible quantum theory differs from both: it is realist, has no parallel universes, and has no primitive collapse.

Hidden variables and Bell’s theorem. The configurations of an indivisible stochastic process play the role that hidden variables played historically, but they are not hidden in the literal sense. The dynamical laws are non-Markovian, and Barandes argues that this permits locality in space to be preserved at the cost of non-Markovianity—a kind of non-locality in time consistent with the light-cone structure of special relativity (Barandes 2025a). This connects with the observation of Glick and Adami that a form of non-Markovianity is intrinsic to even closed quantum systems (Glick and Adami 2020), and with earlier work on causality in EPR by Chang and Cartwright (Chang and Cartwright 1993). Whether this framing evades the full force of Bell’s theorem (Bell 1964) is developed in detail in forthcoming work; it is a central open question.

Many-to-one, like Hamiltonian mechanics. The correspondence is many-to-one in both directions, exactly as that between Newtonian systems and Hamiltonian mechanics. A given Hilbert space can arise from many qualitatively different configuration spaces (one per orthonormal basis), and a given process admits many Hilbert-space representations—an instance of the general underdetermination of ontology by formalism discussed by Curiel (Curiel 2014).

17. Summary

  • An indivisible stochastic process (Definition 33) is a stochastic process whose dynamical laws consist of a single first-order transition map, defined at division events, without an infinite Kolmogorov tower.
  • The free positivity of transition probabilities lets one write (Observation 44), introducing the time-evolution operator with its Schur–Hadamard gauge freedom (Proposition 47).
  • The dictionary (Theorem 50) translates the stochastic process into Hilbert-space language, and the law of total probability’s linearity becomes the linearity of density-matrix evolution and the Born rule (Proposition 51).
  • A Kraus decomposition (Propositions 56–57) and Stinespring dilation (Theorem 59) produce a unitary operator on a space of dimension at most , whose associated transition matrix is unistochastic.
  • The stochastic–quantum theorem (Theorem 62) states that every indivisible stochastic process is a subsystem of a unistochastic process, and the stochastic–quantum correspondence (Corollary 64) runs in both directions.
  • The framework derives the Schrödinger equation, accommodates interference, decoherence, entanglement, and noncommutative observables, and reframes the measurement problem. It comes with two forms of gauge invariance, a Noether theorem, and a natural account of why complex numbers appear.

The most remarkable feature is how little is assumed. From ordinary probability, an old-fashioned configuration space, and a sparse set of first-order transition probabilities—no Hilbert space, no wave function, no unitarity postulate—one recovers the empirical content of quantum theory. Whether the residual non-Markovianity can be reconciled with relativistic locality, and whether the framework yields genuinely new predictions, are the questions that will determine its ultimate significance (Barandes 2025a, 2026).
